name: Caracas
meta_description: TDSC investigative consulting in matters touching Caracas: sanctions-screened due diligence on Venezuelan counterparties, ownership research, risk advisory.
hero_lede: Investigative consulting for matters that touch Caracas, where Venezuela's government, state oil company, central bank and largest private groups are based. Every engagement is screened first for US sanctions compliance and is scoped from Nashville, mostly as lawful due diligence and risk advisory for clients outside Venezuela.
intro: Caracas is Venezuela's capital and its political, financial and corporate centre. The metropolitan area spans five municipalities, Libertador, Chacao, Baruta, Sucre and El Hatillo, and had about 2.9 million residents in the 2011 census, with later estimates of more than five million in greater Caracas. Petroleos de Venezuela (PdVSA), the country's largest company, and Empresas Polar, its largest private group, are headquartered there, as is the Caracas Stock Exchange. Business districts such as El Rosal and Las Mercedes host international companies and embassies, and the city connects to the port of La Guaira and Simon Bolivar International Airport at Maiquetia on the coast.

Organisations commission investigative work connected to Caracas because decisions over oil, minerals, banking and state contracts are concentrated there, and because the sanctions landscape has shifted rapidly since the January 2026 US operation in Caracas in which Nicolas Maduro was captured. OFAC general licences issued through 2026 have reopened questions for oil traders, service companies, banks, investors and creditors: who owns or controls a Caracas counterparty, whether it is linked to blocked persons or state entities, and whether a proposed transaction fits licence conditions. Legacy creditors, arbitration award holders and companies with expropriation claims also need careful, lawful background research.

matters.title: Sanctions-focused counterparty due diligence
matters.text: Research on Caracas-based companies, intermediaries and joint venture partners to establish ownership and control, links to PdVSA, the Government of Venezuela or designated persons, and involvement of parties from excluded jurisdictions, so the client's sanctions counsel can assess whether a proposed dealing fits an OFAC licence.

matters.title: Oil and minerals trade intermediaries
matters.text: Background on traders, shipping agents and service providers presenting themselves as connected to PdVSA or mineral exports from Venezuela, testing claims of authority, corporate history and prior involvement in opaque cargo arrangements, illegal gold supply chains or trade-based money laundering reported in public sources.

matters.title: Creditor and award-holder research
matters.text: Lawful research for holders of Venezuelan sovereign or PdVSA debt, arbitration awards and expropriation claims, mapping state-linked entities and assets outside Venezuela and public court and arbitration records, while respecting licence limits, including OFAC's authorisation of advisory work on restructuring but not settlement.

matters.title: Banking and payment counterparty review
matters.text: Research on Caracas banks and payment intermediaries, including state banks covered by 2026 general licences, using official sanctions lists, published regulatory notices, court records and media, to help compliance teams understand which institutions remain designated and what conditions attach to permitted financial services.

matters.title: Politically exposed person research
matters.text: Reputation and background research on officials, former officials and business figures based in Caracas whose roles may have changed during 2026, covering sanctions designations, foreign indictments, litigation and reported asset holdings abroad, to support onboarding, partnership and reputational risk decisions.

local_context.title: The sanctions perimeter in 2026
local_context.text: The Venezuela Sanctions Regulations remain in force. PdVSA has been on the SDN list since 2019 and the Government of Venezuela was blocked the same year. From January 2026 OFAC issued general licences covering oil exports, diluents, energy services, minerals, contingent investment contracts, negotiations with the government, certain financial services with state banks and advisory work on debt restructuring. OFAC reaffirmed recent licences in August 2026. Conditions and exclusions apply, and policy can snap back quickly.

local_context.title: Licence conditions affecting contracts
local_context.text: Many 2026 licences exclude transactions involving Russia, Iran, North Korea, Cuba and certain China-linked entities, and require payments due to blocked persons to be made into designated Foreign Government Deposit Funds. Some impose reporting obligations, and legal commentary in 2026 noted requirements for contracts with the Government of Venezuela or PdVSA to be governed by US law. These conditions change; TDSC relies on the client's sanctions counsel for each conclusion.

local_context.title: Courts and registries in the capital
local_context.text: Venezuela's highest court, the Supreme Tribunal of Justice, sits in Caracas, and commercial and civil courts for the capital area hear most disputes involving Caracas companies. Company documents are recorded in commercial registry offices serving the capital region, but there is no reliable public online search, so copies are generally obtained in person through Venezuelan counsel. International parties usually prefer arbitration seated outside Venezuela.

local_context.title: Metropolitan structure
local_context.text: Greater Caracas is administratively divided. Libertador municipality forms the Capital District, while Chacao, Baruta, Sucre and El Hatillo belong to Miranda state, and each municipality issues its own business licences and property records. Chacao and Baruta contain much of the corporate office space, including El Rosal and Las Mercedes. Identifying the correct municipality and registry office is a practical first step in verifying a Caracas company or property.

tdsc_approach: As a US company, TDSC screens every matter touching Caracas for sanctions compliance before work begins, identifying each party, its owners and any relationship to PdVSA, the Government of Venezuela or other blocked persons. TDSC does not accept engagements that would violate US or other applicable sanctions, does not provide services to blocked persons and does not advise on avoiding sanctions. Most work is therefore lawful due diligence and risk advisory for clients outside Venezuela, using OFAC and other official lists, foreign registries, court and arbitration records and published reporting. Any record retrieval in Caracas is undertaken only where sanctions counsel confirms it is permitted, through qualified Venezuelan counsel. TDSC has no office in Caracas.

faqs.q: Can TDSC work on a matter involving a Caracas company?
faqs.a: Possibly, after sanctions screening. TDSC first identifies the parties, owners and any links to PdVSA, the Government of Venezuela or designated persons, and asks the client's sanctions counsel to confirm the activity is permitted, for example under a general licence. TDSC declines engagements that would violate US or other applicable sanctions or that would benefit blocked persons.

faqs.q: Have the 2026 OFAC licences lifted sanctions on Venezuela?
faqs.a: No. The licences authorise defined activities, such as certain oil exports, energy services, minerals trade, financial services with some state banks and advisory work on debt restructuring, subject to conditions and exclusions. PdVSA and many individuals remain designated, and OFAC can withdraw licences. Each transaction needs its own legal assessment against current OFAC guidance.

faqs.q: Can TDSC obtain Caracas commercial registry documents?
faqs.a: Where sanctions counsel confirms it is permitted, filings can be obtained in person through qualified Venezuelan counsel, since there is no reliable public online registry search. Many questions can also be answered from foreign registries, court and arbitration records, sanctions listings and published reporting without any activity in Venezuela.

faqs.q: Does TDSC help creditors trace Venezuelan state assets?
faqs.a: TDSC can support creditors' counsel with lawful research on state-linked entities, their assets outside Venezuela and public litigation records. Enforcement and settlement steps involving the Government of Venezuela or PdVSA are restricted by sanctions, and OFAC has authorised restructuring advice but not restructuring itself, so all work is scoped with sanctions counsel.

faqs.q: Does TDSC have staff in Caracas?
faqs.a: No. TDSC has no office, staff or address in Venezuela. Engagements are scoped and managed from Nashville. Where a permitted matter requires document retrieval in Caracas, TDSC works through qualified Venezuelan counsel or professionals identified with the client, within a written scope and only after sanctions screening confirms the work is lawful.
